title: Ruling 2024-03: Sales Tax Applicability to Sales of DNA-Based Ancestry and Health History Reports
text:
Date: July 16, 2024

Written by: Abby Shepard

Approved by: Craig Bolio, Commissioner of Taxes

This is a formal ruling for your client [Taxpayer], regarding the Vermont sales and use tax and corporate income tax. This ruling is based upon representations in your letter dated [Date], including the attached PA-1 power of attorney form.

Facts 

1. [Taxpayer] is a [State]-based company with a distribution center in [State 2] and a specimen-processing laboratory in [State 3]. [Taxpayer] sells its services to both foreign and domestic customers, including customers in Vermont.

2. [Taxpayer] is in the business of selling ancestry and health history reports to customers based on [Taxpayer’s] analysis of DNA in customers’ saliva specimens. Customers order and pay for [Taxpayer’s] services online. [Taxpayer] mails a saliva kit from the [State 2] distribution center to the customer. The customer collects their own saliva specimen using the kit and mails the kit to the laboratory in [State 3]. The laboratory processes the specimen and generates an ancestry and health history report. The customer then accesses their individualized report through [Taxpayer’s] website.

3.The cost of the specimen-collecting kit is generally less than $1.00. The cost of the saliva specimen processing and analysis and the generation of an ancestry and health history report is generally $99.00. The use of the kit is integral to the provision of the service and is consumed in providing the service.

Discussion 

Sales and Use Tax 

1) Type of transaction 

You asked whether the Vermont sales and use tax applies to [Taxpayer’s] sales of DNA-based ancestry and health history reports to Vermont customers. [Taxpayer’s] sales are nontaxable because they include taxable and nontaxable products, and the purchase or sales price of the taxable products is de minimis.

Vermont law imposes sales and use tax on retail sales of tangible personal property in Vermont, unless an exemption applies. 32 V.S.A. §§ 9771, 9773. “Tangible personal property” (TPP) means “personal property that may be seen, weighed, measured, felt, touched, or in any other manner perceived by the senses.” 32 V.S.A. § 9701(7). Although some services are taxable in Vermont, such as admission to places of entertainment and certain telecommunications services, most services are not taxable. 32 V.S.A. §§ 9771, 9773. [Taxpayer’s] services are not of a type that is taxable under Vermont law. [Taxpayer’s] services can only be provided if the customer uses a physical specimen-collecting kit, however, which is taxable TPP when sold at retail, unless an exemption applies.

Under the Vermont sales and use tax rule, “[a] bundled transaction is the retail sale of two or more products, except real property and services to real property, where (1) the products are otherwise distinct and identifiable, and (2) the products are sold for one non-itemized price.” Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3. As a general rule, “if any product included in the bundled transaction would be taxable if sold separately”, then “sales tax must be collected on the selling price of a bundled transaction.” Id. Based on the facts in your letter, it is not clear whether the sales price of [Taxpayer] products is itemized. To be itemized, the sales price must be separately identified on a binding sales document like a receipt. If [Taxpayer’s] transactions are itemized, then the price of the TPP and the service price will not be bundled, and sales tax will only apply to the kit as TPP. If [Taxpayer’s] transactions are not itemized, then sales tax will apply to the entire bundled transaction unless an exception applies.

There are several exceptions to the general rule on bundled transactions that appear to apply to [Taxpayer’s] sales. First, as long as the price of the TPP (the kit) is de minimis, which means 10% or less of the total purchase price, then sales tax will not apply. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3(C)(3). Second, even if the value of the kit is not de minimis, if the true object of the transaction is a nontaxable service, then sales tax will not apply.

A transaction that otherwise meets the definition of a bundled transaction is not considered a bundled transaction if the transaction “includes taxable products and nontaxable products and the purchase price or sales price of the taxable products is de minimis.” Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3(C)(3); see also, 32 V.S.A. § 9741(35). “De minimis” means the seller’s purchase price or sales price of the taxable products is 10% or less of the total purchase price or sales price of the bundled products. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3(C)(3)(a); see also, 32 V.S.A. § 9741(35). A transaction that meets the conditions to be considered de minimis is not taxable. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3(C); see also, 32 V.S.A. § 9741(35). Based on the facts in your letter, [Taxpayer’s] sales include both taxable products (the kit as TPP) and nontaxable products (the report as a service). According to the facts provided, the purchase price or sales price of the taxable products is de minimis, because the kit is 10% or less (the kit’s price is $1.00, which represents 1%) of the total $100 purchase price or sales price of the bundled products. Therefore, [Taxpayer’s] sales would not be considered a bundled transaction and sales tax would not apply.

Even if the de minimis exception did not apply, a transaction that otherwise meets the definition of a bundled transaction is not considered a bundled transaction if the transaction is a retail sale of both (1) TPP and (2) a service; the TPP is essential to the use of the service; the TPP is provided exclusively in connection with the service; and the service is the true object of the transaction. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(4)–3(C)(1); see also, 32 V.S.A. § 9741(35). Based on the facts provided, [Taxpayer’s] retail sales include both TPP (the kit) and a service (the specimen-processing required to produce an ancestry and health history report). The TPP is essential to the use of the service and the TPP is provided exclusively in connection with the service, because the service can only be performed by using the specimen-collecting kit. Additionally, the service is the true object of the transaction, because the customer is paying for the information contained in the report, not for the kit. Therefore, [Taxpayer’s] sales would not be considered a bundled transaction and sales tax would not apply.

2) Location of transaction (situs) 

You asked whether Vermont law considers the sale to have occurred in [State 3], where the specimen-processing occurs, or in Vermont, where the customer receives the kit delivery and presumably uses the service. [Taxpayer’s] Vermont customers take possession of the kit in Vermont and first use services in Vermont, therefore the sale is sourced to Vermont.

The General Sourcing Rules determine whether a sale is sourced to Vermont. Vt. Reg. §§ 1.9701(8)-1–1.9701(8)-3. When the retail sale of product is not received by the purchaser at the seller’s business location, then the sale is sourced to the location where receipt by the purchaser occurs, including the location indicated by instructions for delivery to the purchaser known to the seller. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(8)-3(A)(2). Under the General Sourcing Rules, “receive” and “receipt” mean taking possession of tangible personal property or making first use of services. Vt. Reg. § 1.9701(8)-2(1) and (2). Based on the facts in your letter, [Taxpayer’s] customers must provide instructions for delivery of the kits to the customer in order to collect DNA specimens to send to the [State 3] processing lab. Without a physical delivery address for the customer, then the service cannot be provided. If the instructions to deliver the kit to the customer indicate a location in Vermont, then the sales are sourced to Vermont. Additionally, according to the presumption stated in your letter, customers are making first use of the services in Vermont, so the sales are sourced to Vermont.

3) Use tax 

You asked whether [Taxpayer] owes Vermont use tax on DNA-collecting kits shipped from [State 2] to customers in Vermont. [Taxpayer] does not owe Vermont use tax on the kits to the extent that use tax has already been paid in [State 2] at a rate of at least 6% when [Taxpayer] ships the kits to Vermont customers.

Vermont law imposes a 6% compensating use tax on sales of TPP if the TPP will be used in Vermont, the TPP has not been or will not be subject to the Vermont sales tax, and the TPP is not otherwise exempt. 32 V.S.A. § 9773; Vt. Reg. § 1.9773. A relevant exemption exists for circumstances where retail sales or use tax on the TPP has been paid to another state or jurisdiction, if the other state or jurisdiction allows a corresponding exemption to Vermont’s, and if the other state or jurisdiction’s tax rate is the same or higher than Vermont 6% tax rate. 32 V.S.A. § 9744(a)(3). If Vermont’s tax rate is higher than the other state or jurisdiction’s tax rate, then Vermont tax applies to the extent of the difference in rates. Id. First, based on the facts in your letter, [Taxpayer] ships the kits from [State 2] to be used or consumed by [Taxpayer’s] customers in Vermont. Second, the kits will not be subject to the Vermont sales tax because they are part of a nontaxable sale. Third, [Taxpayer] paid use tax on the kits to [State 2], and [State 2] appears to allow a corresponding exemption to Vermont’s exemption. 32 V.S.A. § 9744(a)(3); U.C.A. § 59-12-104(26). In [State 2] it appears that the use tax rate can be lower than 6%, but depending on the local taxing jurisdiction, can also be much higher. Accordingly, depending on what rate of use tax [Taxpayer] paid in [State 2], [Taxpayer’s] use of the kits may be fully exempt from Vermont use tax or [Taxpayer] may owe use tax on the kits to the extent of the difference in Vermont and [State 2’s] tax rates.

Corporate Income Tax 

In addition to the issues raised in your letter, there may also be corporate income tax implications for the sales [Taxpayer] is making into Vermont. The statements of law provided below are for informational purposes only and do not constitute a position or interpretation taken by the Department on [Taxpayer’s] tax standing or liability. The Department would need a duly executed power of attorney form from [Taxpayer] authorizing us to communicate with you about any corporate income tax implications of sales made within Vermont.

Under Vermont corporate income tax law, a “taxable corporation” is defined in relevant part as a corporation that received any income allocable or apportionable to Vermont. 32 V.S.A. § 5811(15)(C). Taxable corporations are required to file a Vermont corporate income tax return and are subject to the greater of the income tax based on net income or the minimum corporate gross receipts tax. 32 V.S.A. § 5832(1) and (2). A taxable corporation that derives income from sales into Vermont and outside Vermont must apportion its income to Vermont by multiplying Vermont net income by the gross sales or charges for services performed within Vermont, expressed as a percentage of the sales or charges whether within or outside Vermont. Id. 32 V.S.A. § 5833(a). Sales are deemed to be made in Vermont if the corporation’s market for the sales is in Vermont (also called market-based sourcing). 32 V.S.A. § 5833(a)(2). In the case of the sale of a service, the corporation’s market is in Vermont if and to the extent that the service is delivered to a location in Vermont. 32 V.S.A. § 5833(a)(2)(C).

General Provisions 

Issuance of this ruling is conditioned upon the understanding that neither the taxpayer nor a related taxpayer is currently under audit or involved in an administrative appeal or litigation concerning the subject matters of the ruling. This ruling is issued solely to the taxpayer and is limited to the facts presented, as affected by current statutes and regulations.

Other taxpayers may refer to this ruling, when redacted to protect confidentiality, to see the Department's general approach, but the Department will not be bound by this ruling in the case of any other taxpayer or in the case of any change in the relevant statutes or regulations.

This ruling will be made public after deletion of the taxpayer’s name and any information that may identify the taxpayer. A copy of this ruling showing the proposed deletions is attached, and you may request within 30 days that the Commissioner delete any further information that might identify the taxpayer. The final discretion as to deletions rests with the Commissioner.

You have the right to appeal this ruling within 30 days. 3 V.S.A. §§ 808, 815.
